My windows look out across the roofs of a crowded city, and I have come to depend on them. The life I glimpse at my neighbors' windows and on the tar and tin below them often starts my thoughts going, so that half of what I think in a day seems to have begun over there.

Across the way and one story below me, a little boy lives with his father and mother. He has been ill for several weeks now. Long after the rest of the household is up and dressed, he is still in bed, with books and toys heaped about him like drifts. Sometimes he draws his knees up under the covers until they make a snowy mountain, and then he marches a file of paper soldiers up its slope. His kitten has the run of the bed. Some mornings it romps over the counterpane and pounces on his toes. Other mornings it sleeps in a heap on the sunny windowsill and will not be bothered. When he reads, he gives the page such rapt attention that I am sure his book is about far-off islands and coconut trees. In the afternoon someone brings him a tall yellow drink of eggs and milk, and from the way he licks his lips over it I judge that eggnog is one of his favorites. Lately he has taken to pressing his nose eagerly against the window glass, and I take that as the best sign yet that he is getting well.

Now that the days are growing short and the lamps come on early, another set of windows gives me a different sort of entertainment. Their curtains are drawn, and the household shows itself only in shadows: a woman's arm lifting, a man bending to a drawer. Tonight there is hurry behind those curtains, and a good deal of changing of clothes, and I have decided they are getting ready for a party. Presently the upstairs lights will go out, and a few minutes later the family will come out of their door below in shiny evening clothes. I wish them a pleasant dinner, and I hope there is ice cream for dessert. I have a sweet tooth myself.

Opposite me, too, is a kitchen window, where savory dishes simmer on the fire. The cook stirs them with an iron spoon of remarkable length. The old saying holds that whoever sups with the devil needs a long spoon, and this one is long enough that a person dining with the devil could dip safely into the shared pot and never come within reach of him. But surely the proverb has no business on our quiet street.

Many stories lower there is a patch of roof furnished with wicker chairs and a row of bright plants set along the gutter. Every afternoon at exactly six, when that roof has gone into shadow, a man comes out and reads his evening paper. After a while his wife joins him, and they eat their supper from a tray. They sit nearly at the bottom of a well of buildings that shuts them off from the world as completely as the hedge of a fairy garden. When the tray has been carried away they stay on in their chairs. Twilight comes early down there, and like cottagers in a valley they sit and watch the daylight still burning on the peaks above them.

There is another outdoor room on a taller building above me. From where I sit I can see only its bright canvas awning and the side of the trellis that holds it up. On cool summer evenings, I suppose, people sip their coffee up there and watch the lights of the city come on one by one.

So I have glimpses of neighbors all around me: a figure against a curtain, a group about the fire in season, the week's darning left on a rocking chair, a nose at an open window in the morning.

Still, the roofs themselves are the main view. The near ones are graveled and set about with spouts, spinning vents and chimneys, and with posts and clotheslines for the wash. Once a week a laundress puts her head up through a roof scuttle, at very nearly the same minute every time. When the scuttle first begins to stir, there is something mysterious about it, as if one of the forty thieves were pushing at the rocks that guard his cave. But the moment her shoulders clear the opening, her plain, bouncing figure puts an end to the romance. She is a good-natured soul, and when the wind is right I can hear her singing at her work. She tries out the popular tunes with her mouth full of clothespins. Once a pin slipped back into her mouth and nearly choked her.

Farther off, water tanks stand against the sky on the taller buildings, each raised on three supports like fingers holding up a cup. They look to me like buildings newly won over to prohibition, lifting their cups of water to pledge the cause with all a beginner's excitement. The hard liquor, I understand, is kept below, in a rathskeller under the sidewalk and in kegs in the basement. The roof has gone dry in triumph over the cellar.

That row of buildings, with its tanks and towers, shuts off my view to the north. Beyond it lies a crowded world, with the heights of Harlem somewhere among it, but none of that can be seen from my windows.

On summer days the roofs bake in the sun, and spirals of heat rise off them. Tar oozes from the joints of the tin. It is the bright day that brings forth the adder, and it brings out the tar as well. The washing hangs limp on the line. The stockings dangle shriveled and lifeless, nothing like the lively things they are when someone is wearing them. The spouts and chimneys seem to droop under the heavy sunlight, and the spinning vents stop turning. Up there August keeps its hot midsummer rites, as on a steaming altar.
